name: LMV7219M5X_NOPB
title: LMV7219 high-speed comparator, 7 ns, 2.7 V to 5 V supply, push-pull rail-to-rail output
summary: The LMV7219 is a single high-speed, low-power comparator for 2.7 V to 5 V supplies, with 7 mV of built-in hysteresis and a push-pull output that swings to both rails. At 5 V it switches in 7 ns typical while drawing 1.1 mA. Its input common-mode range reaches 200 mV below ground, so it can sense signals at ground. It comes in 5-pin SC70 (DCK) and SOT-23 (DBV) packages.

circuits.title: Typical application: crystal oscillator
circuits.description: A crystal oscillator with fixed values. Two 100 kΩ resistors split VCC to bias the non-inverting input at half supply. The crystal in series with 220 Ω feeds the output back to that input. A 100 kΩ resistor from the output and a 0.1 µF capacitor to ground set the inverting input at a DC level that follows the average output.

circuits.title: Figure 14. Additional hysteresis
circuits.description: Widens the hysteresis past the internal 7 mV with three resistors. The input reaches the non-inverting input through R1; R2 goes from that node to ground and R3 feeds the output back to it. The inverting input sits at VREF. When the output changes state, R3 moves the voltage at the non-inverting input, giving separate rising and falling thresholds. R1, R2 and R3 come from the design equations.

parts.note: positive feedback, from the design equations

notes: The design equations take the output as swinging between 0 and VCC.

circuits.title: Figure 15. Zero-crossing detector
circuits.description: The inverting input is grounded and a 100 mVp-p AC signal drives the non-inverting input, so the output changes state each time the signal passes through 0 V.

circuits.title: Figure 16. Threshold detector
circuits.description: A level detector: the inverting input is held at a reference voltage VREF and the input, divided by R1 and R2, drives the non-inverting input. The output changes state as the divided input crosses VREF.

circuits.title: Figure 17. Crystal oscillator
circuits.description: R1 and R2 from VCC set the DC level at the non-inverting input. The crystal, in series with 220 Ω, closes a positive-feedback path from the output to that input and fixes the frequency. R4 from the output with R3 and C1 to ground set the inverting input at a DC level that follows the average output. The output duty cycle is close to 50 %; resistor tolerance shifts it, and the comparator offset shifts it less.

circuits.title: Figure 18. IR receiver
circuits.description: An infrared photodiode, reverse biased from VCC, passes a current that grows with the infrared light falling on it; that current develops a voltage across RD at the non-inverting input. R1 and R2 divide VCC to set the threshold at the inverting input. The output switches when the RD voltage crosses the divider voltage.

operation.text: A single-supply comparator with built-in hysteresis, about 7 ns delay and 1.1 mA supply current. The common-mode range runs typically from 0.2 V below ground to 1 V under VCC.

The input pair is PNP, so input bias current leaves the device at each input. Taking an input under the lower common-mode limit forward biases the junction between the substrate and the PNP base, and the input bias current rises.

With one input over the upper common-mode limit and the other inside the range, the output still has the right state but the delay grows. With both inputs out of range the input stage saturates and the output state cannot be predicted.
Delay changes little with a large differential input. A differential voltage larger than the supply should not be applied, since it can damage the input stage.
During a transition the output stage briefly conducts from VCC to ground, so a large current flows while it switches. Once it settles, supply current returns to about 1.1 mA at 5 V.

A fixed 7 mV of hysteresis stops the output oscillating when the two inputs sit close together with noise or stray feedback. It moves little with supply or common-mode voltage. It gives one trip point for a rising input and another for a falling one, and as the inputs meet it drives one input quickly past the other, clear of the zone in which it would oscillate, so no external hysteresis resistors are needed.

Three resistors with positive feedback (Figure 14) add hysteresis, at the cost of a slower response. The procedure: pick R3 so its current exceeds the input bias current, checking both output states and using the smaller value; pick the band VHB; compute R1; pick the rising trip point VTHR; compute R2; then check VTHR, VTHF and the hysteresis. The method is meant for adding no more than a few hundred millivolts; past that, R3 is low enough to load the bias divider and R1 may need adjusting.

With the non-inverting input swept up and down (Figure 19), the output goes from VOL to VOH when the input passes VTRIP+ on the way up and returns to VOL when it passes VTRIP− on the way down. VHYST is the gap between the two trip points and VOS lies midway between them.

Runs from one supply or from split supplies, provided the input common-mode voltage keeps the needed headroom below V+; the input range reaches a little below V−. Decouple the supplies to ground with low-inductance capacitors, often ceramic, within 0.5 inch of the pins. Use a ground plane, but remove it close to sensitive pins, for example the inputs.

The part needs high-speed layout. Put a 0.1 µF ceramic capacitor as near V+ as possible, and near V− too with split supplies; a 2.2 µF tantalum capacitor can be added for lower noise. Good bypassing improves stability and removes output chatter. Keep all leads short to cut stray capacitance, lead inductance and parasitic feedback. Solder the part to the board, not into a socket. Use an unbroken, low-inductance ground plane with low-impedance return paths where large currents flow. Route input traces away from output traces, with topside ground between them, and run a ground trace beneath the part as far as the bypass capacitor, screening the inputs from the output. For slow inputs a capacitor of 1000 pF or less between the inputs stops parasitic feedback and oscillation in the transition region, though with a low source impedance it lengthens tpd.
A 1.5 in × 1.5 in two-sided SOT-23 evaluation board carries an unbroken ground plane on its bottom side, with the decoupling capacitors next to the device supply pins.
ESD protection on chip is limited. Store and handle the parts with the leads shorted together or pressed into conductive foam so the MOS gates are not damaged.
